title: Where hyperedges come from (2): inventing them from the data

what.formal: A hypergraph is called **constructed** when the data supplies no groups and the hyperedges are produced by a stated procedure — most commonly by joining each vertex to its $k$ nearest neighbours under some similarity, or by expanding an existing graph. In that case the hypergraph is an artefact of the procedure and its parameters, not a record of the data.
what.plain: Sometimes there are no groups in the data at all — just a table of numbers. Then you have to manufacture the groups yourself, and how you manufacture them decides what the model sees.

what.md: **Why anyone would do this.** Many datasets are tables: a patient with a set of clinical measurements, a point cloud with coordinates, a credit application. There is no relation recorded anywhere. But the rows still resemble each other, and similarity is enough to build structure — join every row to the rows most like it, and call each neighbourhood a hyperedge.

head: Procedure
How the hyperedge is formed
Characteristic weakness
rows: each vertex plus its $k$ most similar vertices
every group has the same size; similarity is forced even where none exists
every pair inside a dense region becomes an edge
quadratic blow-up; the group ceases to be a unit
add an auxiliary vertex per group and connect it
the auxiliary vertex carries no meaning of its own
all vertices of one category, or above a similarity cut
group sizes swing wildly; the threshold is another hidden parameter

what.md: **The consequence to hold onto: the hypergraph is now a hyperparameter.** Two datasets of the same underlying data, processed with $k = 5$ and $k = 50$, are different hypergraphs — different edge degrees, different vertex degrees, different numbers of relations. Every reported number describes one point in that space, and none of the differences came from the data.

This is the sharpest critical question you can put to a paper that constructs its hyperedges: **the choice of construction is a free parameter, so what happens at other settings?** Hold that question; Chapter 7 returns to it with this paper's own numbers.

example.md: **Example 1 — a point cloud becomes a hypergraph.** ModelNet40 is a collection of 3D shapes; each shape is a cloud of points with coordinates. Nothing in it is a relation. This paper turns it into a hypergraph in three steps.

items.md: Convert each point cloud into a table: one row per shape, columns for geometric features.
items.why: Nothing relational has happened yet. This is an ordinary feature matrix, the kind a decision tree would eat directly.

items.md: Measure similarity between rows — here, distance in feature space.
items.why: Similarity is the raw material a constructed hypergraph is made of. It exists whether or not the data intends it: two shapes will always be nearer or farther.

items.md: For each row, take its $k$ nearest neighbours and declare that set of $k+1$ rows one hyperedge.
items.why: The hypergraph now exists. Note precisely what decided its shape: **a distance function and a number $k$**, neither of which came from ModelNet40 itself. Change $k$ and every column of Table I's ModelNet40 row changes.

example.md: **Example 2 — how much a single number moves.** With $|V| = 1{,}000$ rows and $k = 5$, each vertex belongs to 6 hyperedges only if neighbourhoods are perfectly symmetric; in general the count varies. Push $k$ to 50 and every hyperedge grows tenfold while the number of vertices does not move at all.

The honest reading of a constructed hypergraph is therefore: **"this is what the data looks like under the procedure and parameter I chose."** That is not a criticism — it is what any feature engineering is. It only becomes a problem when the paper reports the hypergraph as though it were a property of the dataset. Both Heloc (credit data) and ModelNet40 in this paper's Table I are of this kind.

quiz.q: In a $k$-nearest-neighbour construction, what determines the size of a hyperedge?

opts.md: The number of vertices in the dataset
opts.expl: $|V|$ sets the *number* of hyperedges — one per vertex — but not their size. The two quantities are independent knobs.

opts.md: The parameter $k$: each hyperedge holds the vertex and its $k$ nearest neighbours
opts.expl: Correct, so $k+1$ members. This is why $k$ is the parameter to interrogate: it sets the arity of every relation in the dataset simultaneously, and it is chosen by the experimenter.

Threshold constructions exist (see the table) but that is a different procedure. In plain $k$-NN there is no threshold — you always take exactly $k$, however dissimilar the $k$-th neighbour turns out to be.

quiz.q: A dataset of 800 rows is turned into a hypergraph with $k = 9$. How many members does each hyperedge hold?
quiz.hint: Do not forget the vertex itself — it is part of its own neighbourhood.
quiz.sol: Each hyperedge holds the vertex plus its 9 neighbours: $9 + 1 = 10$ members. Answering 9 is the standard slip, and it is worth catching here because it feeds the degree counts — a vertex is a member of its own hyperedge as well as of the hyperedges its neighbours created.

quiz.q: A paper constructs hyperedges by $k$-NN with $k$ chosen from a small range and reports no experiments at other values. What is the precise nature of the concern?

opts.expl: Nothing suggests an error. The reported numbers may be perfectly correct for the configuration used — the concern is about scope, not accuracy.

opts.md: The results describe one point in a space of possible hypergraphs, and the reader cannot tell how sensitive they are to that choice
opts.expl: Correct, and this is a general habit rather than a quibble about this paper. Whenever a value was chosen by judgement and never varied, the honest report is "this is what happened at the setting we picked". A sensitivity study is what upgrades it to a claim about the method. Chapter 7 lists this among the paper's open questions.

opts.md: The hypergraph should have been native
opts.expl: It could not be — the data had no groups. Constructing them was the only option available, and the question is how that construction was validated, not whether it should have been done.

close: **Where this is going:** whenever a constructed hypergraph is used, the model it feeds is being evaluated on an artefact of a parameter choice. Card 6 turns to the last question in this section: given a hypergraph, why would anyone convert it *back* into a plain graph?
